title: The third time is the signal
caption: Write a skill the third time, once you know what a good result looks like.

first.heading: 1st time: you learn what's needed
first.captainLine: Collect sediment sample: hold 2 m above the seabed…
first.pilotLine: Which depth? What goes on the label?
first.alt: Day 1 in the control room: the captain explains the sediment sample; the pilot asks which depth and which label.

second.heading: 2nd time: you refine it
second.captainLine: Again: check the camera first, lower the arm slowly.
second.alt: Day 2: the captain refines it, the pilot listens; two mugs on the console.

third.heading: 3rd time: you write the skill
third.alt: Day 3: the captain holds the written procedure card out to the pilot; three mugs on the console.

notEnough: Counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, the skill repeats a habit with great confidence.

didYouKnow.label: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: This matches the rule of three from Fowler's Refactoring, a software engineering rule against generalising too early.

story.label: In the story:
story.analogy: Explain the sample, refine it, write the card.

agent.analogy: In Claude Code or Codex: each session starts fresh, so only what you write to a file carries over.

when-to-write-a-skill.header: When to write a skill: Fowler's rule of three
when-to-write-a-skill.description: "The first time you do something, you just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplication thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor." [1] It is a heuristic, not a measured result. The credit to Don Roberts is in the 1999 book, which the research could not read.

fowler-refactoring-slides.title: Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1997 slides)

the-model-as-a-new-employee.header: The model as a new employee: why the rule of thumb holds
the-model-as-a-new-employee.description: Anthropic tells the writer to think of Claude as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows", and to show a prompt to a colleague with minimal context [1]. Anthropic Engineering calls building a skill "like putting together an onboarding guide for a new hire" [2].

anthropic-equipping-agents-with-skills.title: Anthropic Engineering, Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills

where-the-model-is-not-like-a-person.header: Where the model is not like a person
where-the-model-is-not-like-a-person.description: each is backed by a source, but listing them as the breaks is a synthesis: sessions start fresh, so only written files carry over [1]; rules in a file are "context, not enforced configuration" [1]; newer models read instructions more literally [2]; the same words read differently by model [2]; assistants drift toward agreeing with the user [3].

anthropic-claude-memory.title: Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project

sharma-sycophancy.title: Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

three-tries.title: Three tries
three-tries.script: So when does a task become a skill? Think about what you learn each time you explain it to the model. The first time you find out what is needed at all, the second time you tighten it, and by the third time you can tell what a good result looks like, which is the moment you know what you would be writing down.

not-only-repetition.title: Not only repetition
not-only-repetition.script: But counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, you are not capturing a procedure, you are copying a habit, and the skill will repeat your habit with great confidence.

did-you-know.title: Did you know
did-you-know.script: Software engineers arrived at this the same way, long before any AI tool: they call it the rule of three, from Fowler's Refactoring, a rule against generalising too early. I'll leave the exact wording in the notes, because the point here is only that people got there first.
